Distribution of electrons across s, p, d and f subshells, filling lowest energy first.

Atoms of the same element with the same Z but different numbers of neutrons.
Total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
Weighted mean mass of an atom relative to 1/12 of the mass of a ¹²C atom.
Unequal sharing of electrons between atoms of different electronegativity, producing δ⁺ and δ⁻ charges.
Shared pair of electrons between two atoms, often between non-metals.
Both shared electrons originate from the same atom, e.g. NH₄⁺.
Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.
Attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons.
Electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and adopt positions maximising separation.
Atomic radius decreases across a period as nuclear charge increases with no extra shielding, and increases down a group.
A redox reaction in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, as when chlorine reacts with cold dilute sodium hydroxide.
Group 1 and 2 ions give characteristic flame colours as excited electrons fall back to lower levels, emitting specific wavelengths of light.
Group 2 metals react with water with increasing vigour down the group, forming hydroxides and hydrogen gas.
Calcium gives a brick-red flame, strontium a crimson flame and barium a green flame, identifying their compounds.
Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group, so barium hydroxide is far more soluble than magnesium hydroxide.
Group 2 metals burn in oxygen to form basic oxides of formula MO, which react with water to give hydroxides.
Reactivity with water increases down Group 2 because ionisation energies decrease, so the two outer electrons are lost more easily.
Solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group, so barium sulfate is effectively insoluble in water.
Oxidising ability decreases down Group 7, so chlorine displaces bromide and iodide ions from solution but iodine displaces neither.
Reducing ability of halide ions increases down the group as the ions get larger and lose an electron more easily.
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide from solution; chlorine displaces both bromide and iodide ions.
Halogen oxidising power decreases down Group 7, so chlorine displaces bromide and iodide ions from their solutions.
The halogens become less volatile down the group as van der Waals' forces strengthen: chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid, iodine a solid.
The repeating pattern in physical and chemical properties of elements across each period, caused by recurring outer electron configurations.
Acidified silver nitrate gives a white precipitate with chloride ions, cream with bromide and yellow with iodide.
Adding acidified barium chloride solution to a sulfate gives a white precipitate of barium sulfate.
Group 2 carbonates decompose to the oxide and carbon dioxide; stability increases down the group as smaller cations polarise the anion more.
Minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a successful reaction.
k = A e^(−E_a/RT), relating rate constant to temperature and activation energy.
Substance that increases the reaction rate by providing an alternative path of lower activation energy, unchanged at end.
Distribution of molecular kinetic energies in a gas at a given temperature.
rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, where m and n are orders determined experimentally.
Change in concentration of reactant or product per unit time, with units mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
The minimum energy colliding particles need for a reaction to occur; catalysts provide alternative routes with lower activation energy.
The energy needed to break one mole of a given bond in gaseous molecules, averaged over many different compounds.
A state in a closed system where forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations remain constant.
The heat energy change at constant pressure; negative for exothermic reactions and positive for endothermic reactions.
The ratio of equilibrium product to reactant concentrations, each raised to its stoichiometric power; constant at a fixed temperature.
The overall enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken, allowing ΔH to be found from energy cycles.
pV = nRT links pressure, volume and temperature to the number of moles of gas, with all quantities in SI units.
When a condition of an equilibrium system is changed, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.
A curve showing the spread of molecular energies in a gas; the area under the curve equals the total number of molecules.
The amount of substance containing 6.022 × 10²³ particles; one mole of a substance has a mass equal to its Mr in grams.
The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen under standard conditions.
Formed from alkene monomers joining without loss of atoms; e.g. poly(ethene), poly(propene).
Condensation polymers can be hydrolysed (esters/amides break), but addition polymers are largely non-biodegradable.
Polymers formed with elimination of a small molecule (usually H₂O or HCl); e.g. polyester, polyamide.
Polymers can be recycled, incinerated for energy or used as feedstock for cracking, depending on type.
Made from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid (or diacyl chloride); e.g. nylon-6,6 and Kevlar.
Made by reacting a diol with a dicarboxylic acid; e.g. PET from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid.
k = Ae^(−Ea/RT) shows the rate constant growing with temperature and shrinking with larger activation energy.
Comparing initial rates of experiments with different starting concentrations to deduce the order with respect to each reactant.
The power to which a concentration is raised in the rate equation; orders must be found by experiment, not from the balanced equation.
The proportionality constant in the rate equation; it increases with temperature and its units depend on the overall order.
An experimentally determined expression, rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, linking the rate to reactant concentrations raised to their orders.
The slowest step in a mechanism; only species involved up to and including this step appear in the rate equation.
An energy cycle applying Hess's law to ionic compounds, used to calculate lattice enthalpies from measurable enthalpy changes.
The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from an element in its standard state.
A measure of disorder; entropy increases from solid to liquid to gas and when the number of gas molecules increases.
The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms each gain one electron to form 1− ions; exothermic for halogens.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS combines enthalpy and entropy; a reaction is feasible when ΔG is zero or negative.
The enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions; it is strongly exothermic.
Electrons fill lowest energy orbitals first.
Electrons singly occupy degenerate orbitals first.
Energy to remove 1 mol e- from gaseous atoms.
Complex shape; 5 per subshell, 10 e- max.
Dumbbell-shaped orbital; 3 per subshell, 6 e- max.
Spherical orbital holding up to 2 electrons.

Molecule or ion with a lone pair that donates to form a dative bond with a metal centre.
A d-block element that forms at least one stable ion with a partially filled d subshell.

Same structural formula but different spatial arrangement; includes E/Z and optical isomers.
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural arrangement.

Separation by evaporation and condensation; simple for components with very different boiling points.
(Absolute uncertainty / measured value) × 100%; combined by addition for multiplied quantities.
Purification of a solid by dissolving in minimum hot solvent, cooling, filtering and drying.
Heating a reaction in a flask with a vertical condenser so volatile substances do not escape.
Technique using a burette to deliver one solution into a known volume of another to determine concentration.
Forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal rates in a closed system; macroscopic properties are constant.
A catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally; K is unchanged.
K changes with T; for an exothermic forward reaction, K decreases as T rises.
Ratio of product to reactant concentrations each raised to their stoichiometric coefficients at equilibrium.
